cor-proj-gram-colspace.html:
For any n×p matrix A:

  1. N(A⊤A)=N(A);

  2. C(A⊤A)=C(A⊤) and C(AA⊤)=C(A);

  3. rank(A⊤A)=rank(AA⊤)=rank(A);

  4. C(A)⊥=N(A⊤) and Rp=C(A⊤)⊕N(A).

def-proj-blp.title: Best linear predictor
def-proj-blp.html: The best linear predictor of Y given X, written L(Y∣X), is the projection of Y onto L. It is the a+b⊤X that minimizes the mean squared error E(Y−a−b⊤X)2.

def-proj-complement.title: Orthogonal complement
def-proj-complement.html: The orthogonal complement of a subspace S⊆Rn is S⊥={v∈Rn:v⊤u=0 for all u∈S}.

def-proj-ginverse.title: Generalized inverse
def-proj-ginverse.html: A generalized inverse of an m×k matrix A is any k×m matrix A− such that AA−A=A.

def-proj-gls.title: Generalized least squares
def-proj-gls.html: A generalized least squares (GLS) estimate minimizes (y−Xb)⊤V−1(y−Xb). Equivalently, Xβ^GLS=PX,V−1y, and β^GLS solves the generalized normal equations X⊤V−1Xb=X⊤V−1y.

def-proj-leverage.title: Leverage
def-proj-leverage.html: The leverage of observation i is hii=mii, the ith diagonal entry of M. In this context M is often called the hat matrix and written H, because it “puts the hat on” y.

def-proj-ls.title: Least squares
def-proj-ls.html: A vector β^∈Rp is a least squares estimate of β if ‖y−Xβ^‖≤‖y−Xb‖for every b∈Rp. The vector Y^=Xβ^ is the fitted value vector, and ε^=y−Y^ is the residual vector.

def-proj-projection.title: Orthogonal projection matrix
def-proj-projection.html: The orthogonal projection onto a subspace S is the unique n×n matrix PS such that, for every y, PSy∈S and y−PSy⊥S. When S=C(X) for the model matrix of a linear model, we write M=PC(X).

eq-proj-corrected-decomposition.html: ∑i(yi−y¯)2⏟SST=∑i(y^i−y¯)2⏟SSR+∑i(yi−y^i)2⏟SSE,

eq-proj-cosine.html: cos⁡θ=u⊤v‖u‖‖v‖.

eq-proj-distance-split.html: ‖y−u‖2=‖y−y^‖2+‖y^−u‖2.

eq-proj-extra-ss.html: ‖(M−M0)y‖2=‖(I−M0)y‖2−‖(I−M)y‖2=SSE0−SSE.

eq-proj-normal-equations.html: X⊤Xb=X⊤y

eq-proj-partitioned-inverse.html: [(X⊤X)−1]11=(X1⊤(I−M2)X1)−1=(X1⊤X1−X1⊤X2(X2⊤X2)−1X2⊤X1)−1,

eq-proj-population-pythagoras.html: Var(Y)=Var(L(Y∣X))+EU2,Var(L(Y∣X))Var(Y)=σXY⊤ΣXX−1σXYVar(Y).

eq-proj-pythagoras.html: u⊥v⟹‖u+v‖2=‖u‖2+‖v‖2

eq-proj-qr-ls.html: Y^=Q(Q⊤y),Rβ^=Q⊤y,SSE=‖y‖2−‖Q⊤y‖2,hii=∑kqik2.

eq-proj-rank-nullity.html: rank(A)+dim⁡N(A)=p.

eq-proj-three-way.html: ‖y‖2=‖M0y‖2+‖(M−M0)y‖2+‖(I−M)y‖2.

eq-proj-vif-preview.html: Var(β^j)=σ2‖(I−M(j))xj‖2=σ2Sjj(1−Rj2),

exm-proj-ar1.title: Autocorrelated errors
exm-proj-ar1.html: Take eight equally spaced observations with a linear trend and error covariance vst=0.7|s−t|. The V−1-projection onto C(X) is idempotent and self-adjoint for ⟨⋅,⋅⟩V−1 but not symmetric: its largest asymmetry max|pst−pts| is 0.444. The ordinary and generalized slope estimates are 0.648 and 0.650. The listing checks each claim, including that the GLS fit is ordinary least squares on whitened data.

exm-proj-blp.title: A curved mean
exm-proj-blp.html: Let X∼Uniform(0,2) and Y=eX+ε with independent ε∼N(0,0.25). The regression function is not linear, but @thm-proj-blp still identifies a best line. A short calculation gives Cov(X,Y)=1 and Var(X)=1/3, so the population projection has slope 3.000 and intercept 0.195. The listing fits least squares lines to samples of increasing size. The estimates settle on these values, not on any feature of ex. Figure 6.11.1 shows the regression function, the population projection, and a least squares fit.

exm-proj-engel.title: Engel’s food expenditure data
exm-proj-engel.html: Engel’s 1857 survey of 235 Belgian working-class households records annual income and food expenditure. The spread of expenditure grows with income, as Figure 6.9.1(a) shows. Weighting by wi=1/incomei2 (standard deviation proportional to income) changes the fitted slope from 0.4852 to 0.5740. The change in geometry shows up more clearly in the leverages, panel (b). Under ordinary least squares the richest households have the most leverage, with a maximum of 0.255. In the weighted geometry their large variance shrinks their influence, and no household has leverage above 0.037. Whether this is the right geometry depends on whether the variance model holds. Chapter 21 discusses how to check it, and how to get valid standard errors when it fails.

exm-proj-fwl-crime.title: Poverty and murder rates
exm-proj-fwl-crime.html:
For the 50 US states in 2009, regress the murder rate (per 100,000) on the poverty rate, the percentage of single-parent households, and the percentage of the population living in urban areas, with an intercept. The coefficient of poverty is 0.2538. On its own, a simple regression of murder rate on poverty has slope 0.4706, nearly twice as large. Poverty and single parenthood are correlated, and the simple regression gives poverty credit for part of their shared association.

Figure 6.6.1 shows both regressions. Panel (b) is an added-variable plot: the residual of murder rate after regression on the other two regressors and the intercept, against the corresponding residual of poverty. By FWL its least squares slope is exactly the multiple-regression coefficient. The listing confirms the equality to machine precision.

The standard error of the coefficient in the full model is 0.0934. Fitting the residualized regression naively gives 0.0905, smaller by the factor 1.0321, which is (n−1)/(n−4) as predicted.

exm-proj-ginverse-numeric.title: Four answers, one fit
exm-proj-ginverse-numeric.html:
Nine observations fall in three groups of sizes 3,2,4 with group means 5.700, 7.800 and 4.300. The model matrix X=[1,z1,z2,z3] has p=4 columns and rank 3, so X⊤X is singular. We compute β^=GX⊤y for four generalized inverses G of X⊤X: the Moore–Penrose inverse; the inverse obtained by deleting the intercept row and column (@prp-proj-ginverse-exists); the one obtained by deleting the first group’s row and column; and a deliberately strange, non-symmetric one built from the general formula of @exr-proj-all-ginverses.

Generalized inverse β^0 β^1 β^2 β^3 β^1−β^2 max|M−MMP|
Moore–Penrose 4.450 1.250 3.350 -0.150 -2.100 0
drop intercept 0.000 5.700 7.800 4.300 -2.100 1.1×10−16
drop group 1 5.700 0.000 2.100 -1.400 -2.100 1.1×10−16
random -9.102 14.802 16.902 13.402 -2.100 1.8×10−15

The coefficient vectors disagree wildly, including in sign. Yet each produces the same projection matrix up to rounding error, and hence the same fitted values (the group means) and residuals. The difference β^1−β^2 is the same in every row, and so is β^0+β^k for each k. Individual coefficients are not. The trace of M is 3.000, the rank of X.

exm-proj-grunfeld.title: Grunfeld’s investment data
exm-proj-grunfeld.html: Grunfeld’s classic panel follows 11 US firms for 20 years, giving n=220 observations of gross investment, market value and capital stock. With a separate intercept for each firm, the coefficients of value and capital are 0.1101 and 0.3100. The same numbers come from demeaning every variable within firm and fitting two columns. Ignoring the firms altogether (one common intercept) gives 0.1145 and 0.2275 instead. That comparison uses variation between firms, of the sort “large firms invest more”, which the within estimator deliberately discards.

exm-proj-leverage.title: High-leverage states
exm-proj-leverage.html:
Return to the state data, now with all 51 jurisdictions including the District of Columbia, and the model of @exm-proj-fwl-crime. The average leverage is p/n=0.078, and the smallest is 0.021, just above the bound 1/n. The three largest are

Jurisdiction hii multiple of average
District of Columbia 0.506 6.5
Mississippi 0.212 2.7
Alaska 0.177 2.3

The District of Columbia is entirely urban, with by far the highest proportion of single-parent households. It sits at a corner of the regressor cloud that no state comes near, and its leverage is about half the maximum possible. It was omitted from @exm-proj-fwl-crime. @exr-proj-dc asks what happens to the poverty coefficient when it is put back.

exm-proj-line.title: Projections onto a line
exm-proj-line.html: For S=span(v) with v≠0, the single vector v/‖v‖ is an orthonormal basis, so PS=vv⊤v⊤v,PSy=v⊤yv⊤vv. With v=1 this gives P=n−111⊤, the matrix with every entry 1/n, and Py=y¯1. The sample mean is a projection: fitting the intercept-only model replaces every observation by y¯, and the residuals yi−y¯ form a vector in 1⊥, the set of vectors whose entries sum to zero.

exm-proj-oneway-M.title: The one-way layout
exm-proj-oneway-M.html: In the setting of @exm-proj-oneway-rank, sort the observations by group and let group k have nk members. The model space is spanned by the orthogonal vectors z1,…,zg, so by @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula with uk=zk/nk, M=∑k=1gzkzk⊤nk=(n1−11n11n1⊤⋱ng−11ng1ng⊤), a block-diagonal matrix of within-group averaging operators. My replaces each observation by its group mean. The intercept column adds nothing to C(X), so it does not appear, and tr(M)=∑knk/nk=g=rank(X). We got here without a generalized inverse. @thm-proj-M-formula guarantees that any generalized inverse of the singular (g+1)×(g+1) matrix X⊤X produces this same matrix. Section 6.4 checks this numerically.

exm-proj-oneway-rank.title: A rank-deficient layout
exm-proj-oneway-rank.html: Suppose n observations fall into g groups and X=[1,z1,…,zg], where zk is the indicator of group k. Since z1+⋯+zg=1, the vector (1,−1,…,−1)⊤ lies in N(X). The g indicators are linearly independent (their supports are disjoint), so rank(X)=g while p=g+1. By @eq-proj-rank-nullity, N(X) is exactly the line spanned by (1,−1,…,−1)⊤. The model space C(X)=C([z1,…,zg]) is the set of vectors that are constant within groups.

exm-proj-qr-polynomial.title: Polynomial regression
exm-proj-qr-polynomial.html: The columns 1,t,t2,…,td evaluated at 200 equally spaced points in [0,1] become nearly dependent as d grows. To isolate the numerical error, the listing sets y=Xβ exactly for a random β, so that the true least squares solution is β itself. For d=8 the condition number is 6.8×105. The normal equations return β with relative error 1.0×10−5, while QR achieves 1.7×10−11. At d=13, with κ(X)=4.1×109, the normal-equation answer has relative error 9.3×10−1 and not one correct digit, while QR still gets 4.4×10−9. Figure 6.10.1 plots the whole sequence against the reference lines κϵ and κ2ϵ, where ϵ≈2.2×10−16 is machine precision.

exm-proj-sequential-order.title: Order matters
exm-proj-sequential-order.html:
For the state data of @exm-proj-fwl-crime, enter the three regressors after the intercept in two different orders. The listing computes each squared length ‖(Mj−Mj−1)y‖2 directly from the projections.

Order A Order B
poverty 102.49 single-parent 162.84
single-parent 80.04 urban 3.59
urban 0.27 poverty 16.37
residual 101.96 residual 101.96

Entered first, poverty accounts for 102.49 of the corrected total sum of squares 284.76. Entered last, it accounts for only 16.37. The residual sum of squares, and the total explained by all three regressors together (182.80), do not depend on the order, because the final subspace does not. The individual pieces do depend on the order, because the intermediate subspaces differ. Poverty and single parenthood are correlated, so whichever enters first takes the variation they share. The piece for the last regressor is the only one with an order-free meaning. By @thm-proj-fwl, it is the squared length of the projection of y onto the part of that regressor orthogonal to all the others.

exm-proj-simple-nested.title: Intercept inside simple regression
exm-proj-simple-nested.html: Let X0=1 and X=[1,x] with x not constant. Then C(X0)⊥∩C(X) is spanned by the centred regressor x−x¯1=(I−n−111⊤)x, which lies in C(X) and is orthogonal to 1. By @exm-proj-line, M−M0=(x−x¯1)(x−x¯1)⊤Sxx,Sxx=∑i(xi−x¯)2, and so My=y¯1+SxySxx(x−x¯1),Sxy=∑i(xi−x¯)(yi−y¯). Reading off coordinates, the slope is Sxy/Sxx and the intercept is y¯−x¯Sxy/Sxx. These are the familiar formulas, obtained without solving any equations, and the decomposition @eq-proj-three-way becomes ∑iyi2=ny¯2+Sxy2Sxx+SSE.

exm-proj-three-points.title: Three observations
exm-proj-three-points.html: Take responses y=(1,4,2)⊤ at regressor values x=(0,1,3)⊤, with an intercept, so that X=[1,x]. The least squares fit (computed by the listing below) is Y^=(2.143, 2.286, 2.571)⊤,ε^=(−1.143, 1.714, −0.571)⊤, with intercept 2.143 and slope 0.143. Two facts stand out. First, the residual is orthogonal to both columns of X: the entries of ε^ sum to zero, and x⊤ε^=0. Second, the squared lengths add: ‖y‖2=21.000=16.429+4.571=‖Y^‖2+‖ε^‖2. Figure 6.1.1 shows the configuration. The fitted vector is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from y to the plane.

exm-proj-two-factor.title: Additive two-factor model, one observation per cell
exm-proj-two-factor.title_html: Additive two-factor model, one observation per cell
exm-proj-two-factor.html:
Let factor A have a levels and factor B have b levels, with one observation yij for each of the n=ab combinations. Let PA project onto vectors that depend only on the A level, so PAy has entries y¯i⋅, and define PB similarly. Let P0=n−111⊤. Both C(PA) and C(PB) contain 1, so PAP0=PBP0=P0 by @thm-proj-nested.

The crucial computation is PAPB. Averaging over j with i fixed a vector that depends only on j gives the overall average of that vector. So for every y the entries of PA(PBy) are all equal to b−1∑jy¯⋅j=y¯⋅⋅. Therefore PAPB=P0, and so (PA−P0)(PB−P0)=P0−P0−P0+P0=0. The two centred factor spaces are orthogonal. By @thm-proj-sum, the additive model space has projection P0+(PA−P0)+(PB−P0)=PA+PB−P0, and I=P0+(PA−P0)+(PB−P0)+(I−PA−PB+P0) is an orthogonal decomposition with ranks 1, a−1, b−1 and (a−1)(b−1). The residual projection sends yij to yij−y¯i⋅−y¯⋅j+y¯⋅⋅.

The key step used the fact that every A level appears with every B level equally often. If cells are missing or unequally replicated, PAPB≠P0, the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and the sum of squares for A depends on whether B was fitted first. Chapter 17 is about that situation.

exr-proj-M-unique-characterization.title: C1
exr-proj-M-unique-characterization.html: Show that M is the only n×n matrix P satisfying PX=X, P⊤=P and rank(P)=rank(X). Is the rank condition necessary? Is symmetry?

exr-proj-affine-projection.title: A3
exr-proj-affine-projection.html: Let P be an orthogonal projection and a,b real numbers. Show that the eigenvalues of aP+bI are b and a+b. Show that when b≠0 and a+b≠0, (aP+bI)−1=1b(I−aa+bP). Use this to invert the equicorrelation matrix (1−ρ)I+ρ11⊤.

exr-proj-all-ginverses.title: B2
exr-proj-all-ginverses.html:
Let G0 be a generalized inverse of A.

  1. Show that G0+(I−G0A)U+V(I−AG0) is a generalized inverse of A for all conformable U,V.

  2. Show that every generalized inverse G of A has this form. Hint: take U=G−G0 and V=G0A(G−G0), and use A(G−G0)A=0.

  3. Conclude that a matrix has a unique generalized inverse iff it is square and nonsingular.

exr-proj-baseline-change.title: A1
exr-proj-baseline-change.html: A factor with three levels is coded with an intercept and indicators for levels 2 and 3. Write down the matrices T and S of @thm-proj-reparam that convert to the coding in which level 3, rather than level 1, is the omitted baseline, and to sum-to-zero effect coding. Express each new coefficient in terms of the old ones.

exr-proj-colspace-product.title: B2
exr-proj-colspace-product.html: Show that C(AB)⊆C(A), and deduce rank(AB)≤min{rank(A),rank(B)}. Show that C(AB)=C(A) whenever B has full row rank.

exr-proj-complement-basic.title: A1
exr-proj-complement-basic.html: Show that S⊥ is a subspace for any set S (not necessarily a subspace), and that S⊆T implies T⊥⊆S⊥. Show that S⊥=span(S)⊥.

exr-proj-cond-centering.title: C1
exr-proj-cond-centering.html: Let X=[1,x] with x¯=c and Sxx=s2n. Find κ(X) as a function of c, s and n, and show that it grows without bound as c→∞ with s fixed. Show that centring the regressor, a reparameterization, reduces the condition number to max(1,s)/min(1,s).

exr-proj-dc.title: A1
exr-proj-dc.html: Refit the model of @exm-proj-fwl-crime with the District of Columbia included. How does the poverty coefficient change? Draw the added-variable plot and locate the District. Relate what you see to its leverage (@exm-proj-leverage).

exr-proj-dim-formula.title: C1
exr-proj-dim-formula.html: For subspaces S,T⊆Rn, prove dim⁡(S+T)=dim⁡S+dim⁡T−dim⁡(S∩T). Use it to show that two r-dimensional subspaces of Rn with 2r>n must share a nonzero vector.

exr-proj-equal-coefficients.title: B2
exr-proj-equal-coefficients.html: In the model E(Y)=β01+β1x1+β2x2+β3x3 with full-rank X, the hypothesis β2=β3 defines a reduced model with model matrix X0=[1,x1,x2+x3]. Show that the test space C(X0)⊥∩C(X) is spanned by (I−M0)x2, and that (I−M0)x2=−(I−M0)x3. Verify that this agrees with @thm-proj-constraint-space for a suitable P.

exr-proj-equicorrelation.title: A1
exr-proj-equicorrelation.html: Let V=(1−ρ)I+ρ11⊤ with −1/(n−1)<ρ<1. Show that V is positive definite and that C(VX)⊆C(X) whenever 1∈C(X). Conclude that ordinary least squares is generalized least squares for equicorrelated errors in any model with an intercept.

exr-proj-every-solution-ginverse.title: C1
exr-proj-every-solution-ginverse.html: Suppose X⊤y≠0. Show that every least squares estimate b can be written as GX⊤y for some generalized inverse G of A=X⊤X. Hint: with c=X⊤y, try G=G0+(b−G0c)c⊤/(c⊤c). What goes wrong when X⊤y=0?

exr-proj-extra-ss-distance.title: B1
exr-proj-extra-ss-distance.html: With C(X0)⊆C(X), show that SSE0−SSE=‖Y^−Y^0‖2, the squared distance between the two fitted vectors.

exr-proj-fwl-rank-deficient.title: C1
exr-proj-fwl-rank-deficient.html: Drop the full-rank assumption in @thm-proj-fwl. Show that b1 solves the normal equations of the regression of y~ on X~1 iff there exists b2 such that (b1⊤,b2⊤)⊤ is a least squares estimate in the full model.

exr-proj-fwl-residuals.title: B2
exr-proj-fwl-residuals.html: In @thm-proj-fwl, regressing y (not y~) on X~1 gives the coefficient β^1. Show that its residual vector is (I−M)y+M2y, so the residuals are generally wrong even though the coefficient is right.

exr-proj-ginverse-transpose.title: A4
exr-proj-ginverse-transpose.html: Show that if G is a generalized inverse of the symmetric matrix X⊤X, then so is G⊤, and so is GX⊤XG⊤. Which of the four Penrose conditions does the last one satisfy?

exr-proj-gram-schmidt-stability.title: B2
exr-proj-gram-schmidt-stability.html: Implement classical Gram–Schmidt as in @prp-proj-gram-schmidt, and the modified version that subtracts each projection from the working vector before computing the next inner product. For the degree-10 polynomial design of @exm-proj-qr-polynomial, compare ‖Q⊤Q−I‖ for the two and for numpy.linalg.qr.

exr-proj-kruskal.title: B1
exr-proj-kruskal.html: Complete the proof of @thm-proj-A-projection. Show that PX,A is symmetric iff it equals M, and deduce from @thm-proj-kruskal (with V=A−1) that this happens iff AC(X)⊆C(X).

exr-proj-leverage-monotone.title: B2
exr-proj-leverage-monotone.html: Show that adding a column to X cannot decrease any leverage. Show that the leverages in a one-way layout are 1/nk for members of group k, and explain why an observation forming a group on its own has leverage one.

exr-proj-longley-scaling.title: B1
exr-proj-longley-scaling.html: Compute κ(X) for the Longley data (with intercept) as given, after scaling every non-intercept column to unit Euclidean norm, and after centring and scaling. Confirm that the fitted values agree to the precision you expect in all three cases. Which part of the original condition number is “just units”?

exr-proj-moments-fit.title: B1
exr-proj-moments-fit.html: Suppose E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ2I. Show that E(Y^)=Xβ, Cov(Y^)=σ2M, Cov(ε^)=σ2(I−M) and Cov(Y^,ε^)=0. Which of these statements survive when Cov(Y)=σ2V for a general positive definite V?

exr-proj-oblique-norm.title: B2
exr-proj-oblique-norm.html: Let P≠0 be idempotent. Show that the operator norm ‖P‖2=max‖u‖=1‖Pu‖ is at least 1, with equality iff P is symmetric. Hint: if P is not symmetric, find u∈C(P) and v∈N(P) with u⊤v≠0, and consider u+tv for small t.

exr-proj-offdiag.title: B1
exr-proj-offdiag.html: Show that mij2≤mii(1−mii) for i≠j, and hence |mij|≤1/2. When is the bound attained?

exr-proj-oneway-spaces.title: B1
exr-proj-oneway-spaces.html: A one-way layout has three groups of sizes 2,2,1 and model matrix X=[1,z1,z2,z3]. Find bases for C(X), N(X), C(X⊤) and C(X)⊥, and check that the dimensions agree with @eq-proj-rank-nullity and @thm-proj-direct-sum.

exr-proj-partial-correlation.title: B3
exr-proj-partial-correlation.html: For a single regressor xj, the partial correlation of y and xj given the other regressors is the sample correlation of y~ and x~j (both residualized on X(j), which contains 1). Let t=β^j/se(β^j) with se(β^j)2=SSE/[(n−p)‖x~j‖2]. Show that the squared partial correlation equals t2/(t2+n−p).

exr-proj-penrose.title: B3
exr-proj-penrose.html: Using the singular value decomposition, show that (X⊤X)+X⊤=X+ and XX+=M. Show also that X+=(X⊤X)−1X⊤ when X has full column rank.

exr-proj-product.title: B1
exr-proj-product.html: Let P1,P2 be orthogonal projections. Show that P1P2 is an orthogonal projection iff P1P2=P2P1, and that in this case it projects onto C(P1)∩C(P2). Hint: for the range, show P1P2u=u iff u lies in both subspaces.

exr-proj-r2-affine.title: A2
exr-proj-r2-affine.html: Show that, for a model with 1∈C(X), R2 is unchanged when y is replaced by a1+by with b≠0, and when any column of X is replaced by an affine function of itself. Is it unchanged when a regressor is replaced by its logarithm?

exr-proj-r2-null-distribution.title: C1
exr-proj-r2-null-distribution.html: Suppose Y∼Nn(μ1,σ2I) and 1∈C(X) with rank(X)=r. Using the results of Chapter 4, show that R2∼Beta((r−1)/2,(n−r)/2), so that E(R2)=(r−1)/(n−1) even though no regressor is related to the response. Use this to motivate the adjusted R2=1−(1−R2)(n−1)/(n−r).

exr-proj-residual-sum.title: A2
exr-proj-residual-sum.html: Show that the residuals sum to zero whenever 1∈C(X), even if no column of X is constant. Give an example of a model without such a column in which this happens, and one in which the residuals do not sum to zero.

exr-proj-side-conditions.title: B2
exr-proj-side-conditions.html: Let rank(X)=r<p and let C be a (p−r)×p matrix. Show that the constrained problem “minimize ‖y−Xb‖ subject to Cb=0” has a unique solution for every y, and that its fitted values are My, iff rank(XC)=p. Show that the condition implies C(C⊤)∩C(X⊤)={0}, and interpret: the constraints must not restrict any estimable function.

exr-proj-simple-leverage.title: A1
exr-proj-simple-leverage.html: For simple regression, derive hii=n−1+(xi−x¯)2/Sxx directly from @exm-proj-simple-nested, and show that the largest leverage belongs to the observation with xi farthest from x¯.

exr-proj-small.title: A1
exr-proj-small.html: Let S=span{(1,1,0)⊤,(0,1,1)⊤}. Compute PS in two ways: by Gram–Schmidt and @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula, and by @thm-proj-M-formula. Verify symmetry, idempotence and trPS=2. Find S⊥ and check that I−PS projects onto it.

exr-proj-spectral-converse.title: A2
exr-proj-spectral-converse.html: Show that a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues all lie in {0,1} is an orthogonal projection. Give a non-symmetric 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues 0 and 1 that is not idempotent, and one that is idempotent.

exr-proj-three-points-M.title: A1
exr-proj-three-points-M.html: For @exm-proj-three-points, write out the 3×3 matrix M with exact fractional entries, verify trM=2, and recover the fitted values and residuals quoted in the text.

exr-proj-two-factor-interaction.title: C1
exr-proj-two-factor-interaction.html: Extend @exm-proj-two-factor to m≥2 observations in every cell and a model with interaction. Find five mutually orthogonal projections summing to I, corresponding to the grand mean, factor A, factor B, the interaction, and within-cell error, and find their ranks. Describe the action of each on y in terms of cell, row, column and grand means.

exr-proj-two-factor-numeric.title: A1
exr-proj-two-factor-numeric.html: Construct the projections PA, PB and P0 of @exm-proj-two-factor for a=3, b=2 and verify PAPB=P0 numerically. Delete one observation and recompute. Show that the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and find the largest entry of (PA−P0)(PB−P0).

exr-proj-uncentred-r2.title: B1
exr-proj-uncentred-r2.html: Show that if 1∈C(X) then R02=‖Y^‖2/‖y‖2=(ny¯2+SSR)/(ny¯2+SST)≥R2. Construct a data set and a model without an intercept for which R02>0.95 but the model’s residual sum of squares exceeds that of the intercept-only model.

exr-proj-vif.title: B1
exr-proj-vif.html: Let xj be a column of X, let X(j) be X with that column removed, and assume 1∈C(X(j)). Show that ‖(I−M(j))xj‖2=Sjj(1−Rj2), where Rj2 is the R2 from regressing xj on X(j). Deduce @eq-proj-vif-preview.

exr-proj-wls-leverage.title: B3
exr-proj-wls-leverage.html: For weighted least squares, V=diag(1/w1,…,1/wn) with wi>0. Show that the diagonal entries of PX,V−1 equal those of the orthogonal projection onto C(W1/2X), where W=diag(wi), and that they sum to rank(X). Interpret them as leverages.

lem-proj-complement-intersection.html: For subspaces S1,S2⊆Rn, (S1+S2)⊥=S1⊥∩S2⊥and(S1∩S2)⊥=S1⊥+S2⊥.

lem-proj-fwl-split.title: Orthogonalizing a partitioned model space
lem-proj-fwl-split.html:
Under the assumptions above:

  1. C(X)=C(X2)⊕C(X~1), and the two summands are orthogonal;

  2. X~1 has full column rank;

  3. M=M2+M~1, where M~1=X~1(X~1⊤X~1)−1X~1⊤.

lem-proj-ginverse-invariance.html:
Let X be n×p and let G be any generalized inverse of X⊤X. Then:

  1. XGX⊤X=X and X⊤XGX⊤=X⊤;

  2. XGX⊤ does not depend on the choice of generalized inverse;

  3. XGX⊤ is symmetric, even when G is not.

lem-proj-null-colspace.html: For any n×p matrix A, N(A⊤)=C(A)⊥andN(A)=C(A⊤)⊥.

prp-proj-A-selfadjoint.html: An idempotent matrix P is the A-orthogonal projection onto C(P) iff AP is symmetric, that is, iff ⟨Pu,v⟩A=⟨u,Pv⟩A for all u,v.

prp-proj-conditional-expectation.html:
Let m(X)=E(Y∣X) with EY2<∞. Then:

  1. m(X) is the projection of Y onto G. It minimizes E(Y−g(X))2 over g, and E[(Y−m(X))g(X)]=0 for all g(X)∈G;

  2. L(Y∣X)=L(m(X)∣X): the best linear predictor of Y equals the best linear predictor of the regression function;

  3. E(Y−L(Y∣X))2=E(Y−m(X))2+E(m(X)−L(Y∣X))2;

  4. if m is affine, m(X)=L(Y∣X).

prp-proj-consistency.title: Consistency for the projection
prp-proj-consistency.html: Let (Xi,Yi), i=1,2,…, be independent copies of (X,Y) with finite second moments and ΣXX positive definite. Let (α^n,β^n) be the least squares coefficients from the first n observations, with an intercept. Then (α^n,β^n)→(α∗,β∗) with probability one. No assumption about the form of E(Y∣X), the distribution of the errors, or their variance is needed.

prp-proj-fit-residual.html:
For any data vector y:

  1. X⊤ε^=0 and Y^⊤ε^=0;

  2. if 1∈C(X) (for example, the model has an intercept), then ∑iε^i=0 and the mean of the fitted values is y¯;

  3. ‖y‖2=‖Y^‖2+‖ε^‖2;

  4. ‖ε^‖2=y⊤(I−M)y and ‖Y^‖2=y⊤My;

  5. if y=Xβ+ε for some β, then Y^=Xβ+Mε and ε^=(I−M)ε.

prp-proj-ginverse-exists.title: Existence
prp-proj-ginverse-exists.html: Every matrix has a generalized inverse. If A has rank r and is permuted so that A=(A11A12A21A22) with A11 an r×r nonsingular block, then A−=(A11−1000) (permuted back) is a generalized inverse.

prp-proj-gram-schmidt.title: Gram–Schmidt
prp-proj-gram-schmidt.html: Let v1,…,vk be linearly independent. Define recursively wj=vj−∑i<j(ui⊤vj)ui,uj=wj/‖wj‖,j=1,…,k. Then each wj≠0. The vectors u1,…,uk are orthonormal, and span(u1,…,uj)=span(v1,…,vj) for every j.

prp-proj-leverage.title: Properties of leverage
prp-proj-leverage.html:
Let rank(X)=r, and let ei denote the ith standard basis vector. Then:

  1. hii=‖Mei‖2=∑jmij2, the squared length of the projection of ei onto C(X);

  2. 0≤hii≤1, and ∑ihii=r, so the average leverage is r/n;

  3. if 1∈C(X), then hii≥1/n;

  4. hii=1 iff ei∈C(X). In that case y^i=yi for every y, the ith residual is always zero, and mij=0 for j≠i;

  5. if X=QR with Q having orthonormal columns spanning C(X), then hii is the squared length of the ith row of Q.

prp-proj-leverage-mahalanobis.html: Under these assumptions, hii=1n+(x(i)−x¯)⊤(X~1⊤X~1)−1(x(i)−x¯), where x(i) is the ith row of X1, written as a column vector.

prp-proj-min-norm.title: Minimum-norm least squares
prp-proj-min-norm.html: β^+=X+y is a least squares estimate, and it has the smallest Euclidean norm among all least squares estimates.

prp-proj-oblique.html: Let P be idempotent. Then Rn=C(P)⊕N(P), and P maps each y=u+v (u∈C(P), v∈N(P)) to u. Conversely, for any decomposition Rn=S⊕T there is exactly one idempotent P with C(P)=S and N(P)=T, the projection onto S along T. It is an orthogonal projection iff T=S⊥, that is, iff P is symmetric.

prp-proj-orthonormal-formula.html: Let the columns of the n×r matrix Q be an orthonormal basis for S, so that Q⊤Q=Ir. Then PS=QQ⊤=∑i=1ruiui⊤, where u1,…,ur are the columns of Q.

prp-proj-trace-rank.title: Spectrum, rank and trace
prp-proj-trace-rank.html:
Let P be the orthogonal projection onto an r-dimensional subspace S. Then:

  1. every eigenvalue of P is 0 or 1, and 1 has multiplicity r;

  2. rank(P)=tr(P)=r;

  3. Pv=v iff v∈S, and Pv=0 iff v∈S⊥;

  4. v⊤Pv=‖Pv‖2≤‖v‖2, so P and I−P are nonnegative definite.

thm-proj-A-projection.html: Let A be positive definite and X any n×p matrix. The A-orthogonal projection onto C(X) is PX,A=X(X⊤AX)−X⊤A, for any generalized inverse. It satisfies PX,A2=PX,A and C(PX,A)=C(X), and the matrix APX,A is symmetric. The matrix PX,A itself is symmetric iff AC(X)⊆C(X), and in general it is not.

thm-proj-M-formula.html: For any n×p matrix X and any generalized inverse (X⊤X)−, M=X(X⊤X)−X⊤ is the orthogonal projection onto C(X). In particular rank(M)=tr(M)=rank(X). If X has full column rank, M=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤.

thm-proj-blp.html: Let μX=EX, μY=EY, ΣXX=Cov(X) and σXY=Cov(X,Y), and suppose ΣXX is positive definite. Then L(Y∣X)=α∗+β∗⊤X,β∗=ΣXX−1σXY,α∗=μY−β∗⊤μX. The prediction error U=Y−L(Y∣X) has mean zero and is uncorrelated with every component of X. Moreover Var(Y)=Var(L(Y∣X))+EU2,Var(L(Y∣X))Var(Y)=σXY⊤ΣXX−1σXYVar(Y).{#eq-proj-population-pythagoras}

thm-proj-constraint-space.html: Let M project onto C(X) and let P be an n×q matrix. If S0=C(X)∩N(P⊤), then S0⊥∩C(X)=C(MP). Hence the projection onto S0 is M−PC(MP), and dim⁡S0=r−rank(MP).

thm-proj-direct-sum.title: Orthogonal decomposition
thm-proj-direct-sum.html: For every subspace S⊆Rn, Rn=S⊕S⊥,dim⁡S+dim⁡S⊥=n,(S⊥)⊥=S. Hence every y∈Rn can be written uniquely as y=u+v with u∈S and v⊥S.

thm-proj-fwl.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell
thm-proj-fwl.html:
Let β^=(β^1⊤,β^2⊤)⊤ be the least squares estimate in the full model. Then:

  1. β^1=(X~1⊤X~1)−1X~1⊤y~=(X~1⊤X~1)−1X~1⊤y. So β^1 is the coefficient from regressing y~ (or y itself) on X~1;

  2. the residual vector from regressing y~ on X~1 equals the residual vector (I−M)y of the full model;

  3. β^2=(X2⊤X2)−1X2⊤(y−X1β^1).

thm-proj-invariant-functions.html: For λ∈Rp, the value λ⊤β^ is the same for every least squares estimate β^ (and every y) iff λ∈C(X⊤), that is, iff λ⊤=ρ⊤X for some ρ∈Rn. In that case λ⊤β^=ρ⊤My.

thm-proj-kruskal.title: Kruskal
thm-proj-kruskal.html: For positive definite V, My=PX,V−1y for every y iff C(VX)⊆C(X).

thm-proj-ls-projection.title: Least squares is projection
thm-proj-ls-projection.html: A vector β^ is a least squares estimate of β iff Xβ^=My. Consequently the fitted values Y^=My and residuals ε^=(I−M)y are the same for every least squares estimate.

thm-proj-nested.title: Nested projections
thm-proj-nested.html:
If C(X0)⊆C(X), then:

  1. MM0=M0M=M0;

  2. M−M0 is the orthogonal projection onto C(X0)⊥∩C(X), the orthogonal complement of C(X0) within C(X);

  3. rank(M−M0)=r−r0;

  4. (I−M0)−(I−M)=M−M0, and M0(M−M0)=(M−M0)(I−M)=0.

thm-proj-normal-equations.title: Normal equations
thm-proj-normal-equations.html:
The normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y{#eq-proj-normal-equations}

are consistent for every y, and their solutions are exactly the least squares estimates. One solution is β^=(X⊤X)−X⊤y, for any generalized inverse, and the set of all solutions is β^+N(X)={β^+v:Xv=0}. In particular, the least squares estimate is unique iff rank(X)=p, and then β^=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.

thm-proj-projection-theorem.title: Projection theorem
thm-proj-projection-theorem.html: Let S be a subspace of Rn and y∈Rn. There is exactly one y^∈S such that ‖y−y^‖≤‖y−u‖for all u∈S. It is the unique y^∈S with y−y^⊥S. Moreover, for every u∈S, ‖y−u‖2=‖y−y^‖2+‖y^−u‖2.{#eq-proj-distance-split}

thm-proj-r2-cosine.html: Assume 1∈C(X) and y∉span(1). Let θ be the angle between the centred response y−y¯1 and the centred fitted vector Y^−y¯1. Then R2=cos2⁡θ=corr(y,Y^)2, where corr is the sample correlation. For simple regression on one regressor x, R2=corr(y,x)2.

thm-proj-reparam.title: Invariance under reparameterization
thm-proj-reparam.html: Let X (n×p) and W (n×q) satisfy C(X)=C(W). Then the two linear models E(Y)=Xβ and E(Y)=Wγ have the same projection M, the same fitted values and residuals for every y, and the same residual sum of squares. There are a p×q matrix T with W=XT and a q×p matrix S with X=WS. If γ^ is a least squares estimate for W, then Tγ^ is one for X, and Sβ^ is one for W whenever β^ is one for X. If both matrices have full column rank, then p=q, T=S−1, and γ^=Sβ^.

thm-proj-sum.html: Let P1,P2 be orthogonal projections. Then P1+P2 is an orthogonal projection iff P1P2=0, that is, iff C(P1)⊥C(P2). In that case it projects onto C(P1)⊕C(P2).

thm-proj-sym-idem.html: An n×n matrix P is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace iff P⊤=P and P2=P. In that case the subspace is C(P), and I−P is the orthogonal projection onto C(P)⊥.
